title: Kernel leapfrog occupancy shadow scan (Nsight captures) — Apr 2025
body:
Quick notes from the 3 capture runs (nsight) I did on Apr 10–14 while chasing the low-occupancy / intermittent tail-latency regressions for short-context microbatches. Purpose: find why SM active time dips to ~60–70% for 8-token requests even when overall GPU utilization looks fine, and why CUDA graph replay sometimes clusters tiny kernels and amplifies tail latency.

Summary / hypothesis (short):
- We see a behavior I’m calling ‘kernel leapfrogging’ where short kernels (kv read/write, tiny matmuls for head-specific ops) get interleaved by the driver such that most SMs are idle between kernel launches.
- CUDA graph capture/replay can exacerbate the effect by re-ordering / batching kernel launches in a way that produces long quiet windows on SMs (launch clustering).
- Root causes likely: (1) inefficient streaming of small kernels across SMs (launch serialization), (2) kernel resource imbalance (register/sharedmem per-block prevents higher resident CTAs), and (3) attention/softmax kernels not fused optimally for short sequence lengths.

Experiment harness (what I ran):
- Model: trimmed decoder-only 8B-ish reference (fp16), config: 16 heads, 64 head-dim, KV cache enabled.
- Worker: dedicated A100-40GB, driver 525.x, cuda 12.1, cuDNN not relevant (custom kernels).
- Workload: microbatch = 1 request x batch-size 2, sequences: 8 tokens (short), then moved to 32 tokens to compare.
- Batching policy: continuous batching disabled for these runs to observe raw kernel patterns; repeated runs with batching enabled showed different behavior (see notes).
- Capture tool: Nsight Systems timeline capture (trace, 200ms windows), and Nsight Compute for hotspot analysis on key kernels.
- CUDA graph: compared 3 modes — no graph, graph-capture-per-step, and global-graph-replay.

Nsight capture parameters:
- Metric sets: sm__throughput.avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_active, sm__warps_active.avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_active, l2_subpector_bandwidth.avg, achieved_occupancy, warp_efficiency
- Sampling: timeline traces with high-res kernel timings, API trace enabled to see launches and stream IDs.
- Filters: kernel name patterns: decoder_step*, kv_cache_*, softmax*, matmul_*_fp16, layernorm*

Key observations (detailed):
1) Occupancy vs utilization mismatch
- Achieved occupancy reported by Nsight for matmul kernels: 0.28–0.36 (28–36%) for short sequences; theoretical max occupancy for kernel config would allow ~0.75–0.85 if register/sharedmem were lower.
- SM active time: 62–71% during 8-token runs (avg), while warp efficiency per-active-SM remained ~84–90%. This indicates SMs that are active are doing useful work, but many SMs sit idle.

2) Launch clustering & quiet windows
- Timeline showed kernel launches clustered into small bursts followed by quiet windows of 200–800 us. Clusters correspond to groups of small kernels that are launched sequentially on the same stream and finish quickly, but the driver’s dispatch inter-cluster gap leaves SMs idle.
- With CUDA graph global capture, clusters were larger (more kernels coalesced) and quiet windows became more pronounced — overall lower SM active duty cycle.

3) Kernel-level imbalance (leapfrog)
- Decoder step decomposed into 4-6 tiny kernels (kv read, per-head matmul, softmax, kv write). The per-head matmuls are launched per-head, so we get many tiny kernel launches instead of a fused multihead matmul; this creates ~N_heads kernels that are short (10–50 us).
- Because register usage per-thread-block is high, the matmul kernel only fits ~2 CTAs per SM, limiting occupancy even if the kernel were larger.

4) Memory staging stalls (L2 / H2H)
- KV cache write path shows bursts of device-to-device memcpy and periods where L2 bandwidth saturates briefly then drops. Hostcopy (when present) creates additional jitter.
- Prefetch windows are misaligned with kernel boundaries; when async copies start slightly late they block subsequent kernels on the same stream, pushing work later and enlarging quiet windows.

5) Tail latency correlation
- The long quiet windows map to the percentiles in request tail-latency (p95–p99). Replays using larger CUDA graph batches pushed p99 higher by ~20–30% in our microbatch short-sequence tests.

Metric excerpts (representative):
- 8-token run (no graph): achieved occupancy (avg) 33%, SM active time 67%, warp efficiency 88%, avg kernel duration 35 us (for tiny matmuls), launch interval jitter 20–40 us.
- 8-token run (global CUDA graph): achieved occupancy 29%, SM active time 59%, warp efficiency 86%, avg kernel duration 33 us, cluster quiet gap 300–700 us.
- 32-token run (no graph): achieved occupancy 71%, SM active time 88%, warp efficiency 91%, avg kernel duration 800 us.

Interpretation / why this matters:
- For short context requests, tiny per-head kernels are dominating the timeline. Even though these kernels are efficient per-SM when active, their short duration and sequential launches leave many SMs idle most of the time: low occupancy despite healthy warp efficiency.
- CUDA graph replay tends to cluster launches in a way that increases quiet gaps; while graph replay reduces CPU overhead, it can hurt SM-on-duty-time for microbatch patterns unless capture boundaries and kernel fusion are tuned.

Hypotheses to test (next runs):
1) Fuse per-head matmul into a single kernel where possible (multihead kernel) to increase per-kernel runtime and improve occupancy.  --> PR/experiment H1.
2) Reduce register pressure in the matmul kernel to allow more CTAs per SM (compiler flags / kernel rewrite) --> H2.
3) Capture graphs at a coarser boundary (per-block-of-steps) rather than global graph to avoid replay clustering tiny kernels; compare p99. --> H3.
4) Use persistent-kernel model for the shortest-sequence codepath (persistent CTA that pulls work) to eliminate launch overheads. --> H4.
5) Introduce microbatch aperture (delay window) to coalesce short requests in user-space into larger effective kernels (trade latency vs SM duty). --> H5.

Immediate actions & owner assignment: 
- Diego: prototype a fused multihead matmul for the short-seq codepath (PR + perf test) — link to bench in github PR 498 as reference. (JIRA-INF-3412)
- Claire: run nsight captures with register-pressure-reduced builds (lower unrolling) to measure occupancy improvement by Apr 22. Add Nsight Compute sections for achieved_occupancy and regs_per_thread. (CONFLUENCE-1234)
- Evan: try graph-capture boundary changes (capture-per-step vs capture-per-block) and record p50/p95/p99 across runs; test with batching on/off. Report in JIRA ticket.

Notes from quick micro-experiment I ran while drafting:
- Modified matmul kernel launching 1 fused multihead vs per-head (toy change) — resident CTAs increased from 2->4 per SM, achieved occupancy jumped 33%->56% for 8-token run, p95 decreased ~6% and p99 decreased ~12% in that trial (small sample). This supports H1.

Risks & tradeoffs: 
- Fusing kernels increases binary complexity and might raise register/sharedmem usage which could negate occupancy gains; we need iterative profiling.
- Persistent kernels reduce launch overheads but complicate concurrency (preemption) and interact badly with prefetch windows.
- Increasing microbatch aperture trades single-request latency for better throughput/SM utilization; must be opt-in / policy-controlled.

Open questions / things to capture next run:
- Exact register per-thread numbers on matmul kernels across compilers (nvcc 12 vs 13) — might be a compiler regression or flag-dependent.
- Can we schedule small kernels on separate low-priority streams to allow larger kernels to run uninterrupted? (stream priority experiments needed)
- How do different GPU models (H100 vs A100) behave — is launch latency vs kernel runtime different enough to change the break-even point?

Files/links to attach to ticket: nsight timeline captures (raw) — run IDs: run-20250410-01, run-20250412-03, run-20250414-02. I uploaded the compressed timelines to the Confluence page (CONFLUENCE-1234).
